title: Prevalence of vitamin A deficiency and dietary patterns identified using latent class analysis in children aged 6–59 months in a food-insecure setting in the Democratic Republic of the Congo: A cross-sectional study
content:
by Landry Egbende, Ingunn M. S. Engebretsen, Branly Mbunga, Josué Lukusa, Pierrot L. Tugirimana, Mala Ali Mapatano, Pierre Z. Akilimali

Vitamin A deficiency (VAD) remains a major public health problem in sub-Saharan Africa. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Vitamin A supplementation (VAS) was introduced more than two decades ago. However, the nutritional situation of children in the DRC remains worrying. Given the lack of up-to-date national data on VAD and the limited evidence from highly food-insecure settings, context-specific data are needed to better understand the burden of VAD and its dietary determinants. A cross-sectional study was conducted from 5 May 2025 to the 1st of June 2025 in the province of Kasai Oriental, among 420 children aged 6–59 months. Participants were selected using a multistage sampling approach. The prevalence of VAD was estimated as the proportion of participants with serum retinol concentrations below 0.70 µmol/L. Additionally, latent class analysis was used to identify dietary patterns. Associations between explanatory variables and serum retinol concentrations were assessed using multivariate gamma regression. This study found that the prevalence of VAD was 14.5% (95% CI: 11.5–18.2). Approximately two-thirds of children (64%) were classified in the low plant-source vitamin A diet class, and the majority of children (96%) were classified in the low animal-source vitamin A diet class. The gamma regression analysis found that children in the low animal-source vitamin A diet class had a 13% lower mean serum retinol ratio compared with those in the animal-source vitamin A-rich diet class (mean ratio [MR] =0.87;95%CI:0.75-1.01; p = 0.050), and children living in food-secure households had a 13% higher mean serum retinol ratio than those from food-insecure households (MR = 1.13;95%CI:1.01-1.28; p = 0.048). VAD remains a moderate public health problem in this highly food-insecure setting in the DRC. The importance of dietary patterns suggests that current strategies may need to be reoriented, emphasizing dietary intake and food security.
